per_object_cap.stated: 1 GB of storage included on Free, then USD 1.50 per additional GB; no per-database cap is published, because the limits are per workspace and split across unlimited databases

retention.notes: the free column states 1 day of backup retention; that is a backup window and not a data-retention clock

egress.terms: no egress allowance and no per-GB transfer line is published; the metered quantity is query tokens and storage

the FAQ answers, captured through the search index because the page renders them collapsed: 'No, the db never pauses. We don't have any cold start time on the free tier.'; 'most limits are per workspace'; 'You can typically pay for additional capacity without having to move to a higher tier. This is true even when you are on the free tier.'
the architecture claim the free tier rests on: storage and compute are decoupled and the database 'scales to zero with no cold start time'

record.notes: A query token is an abstract unit of CPU and memory. The page defines it but does not convert it, so the allowance cannot be expressed in rows or bytes. That is a discretionary meter in the sense that matters. There is no ceiling a reader can design against, only a price per unit. Two properties make the tier more useful than such a ceiling suggests. The limits are per workspace across unlimited databases, so tenant count is not the constraint. Reaching the limit is an overage and not a refusal. No inactivity or expiry policy is published. The free tier is the only one in this topic where the vendor states that it never pauses.
record.binding_note: the token counter is the only hard meter. Storage and connections overage are both purchasable on the free tier without changing plan, and no pause or deletion is published, so the counter is what a reader designs against.
